whatTheyArgued: Begriffsschrift section 11 (verbatim snip, German, archive.org): the concavity with its German letter marks the domain of the generality; only inside that domain does the letter hold its meaning, and the same letter may occur in different domains without meaning carrying across. In On Sense and Reference (1892; not on disk) the morning and evening star share a reference but differ in sense, which explains why the identity statement is informative (SEP).

scholarship.supports: quantifiers as variable-binding; morning/evening star as same denotation, different senses; reference as a relation between expression and object
scholarship.disputes: entry gives no equivalence-class account of reference; I read it via a summariser and did not check the sections myself

ourUse: scoped-kind.js: a quantifier-bound reference resolves to a pattern/Kind, not a particular. aliases.js: the referent is the equivalence class of aliases; identity is a byte key over the class, never a spelling.

bends.ours: Quantifier scope used to route 'every farmer who owns a donkey ... it' to Kind.
bends.theirs: The snip concerns variable scope in his formal language. The donkey-sentence analysis is later linguistics, not Frege.

bends.ours: 'reference is an equivalence class, never a spelling'; aliases are interchangeable forms.
bends.theirs: He says co-referring names can differ in sense and cognitive value; an alias class erases exactly that. 'Equivalence class' is not in the SEP account of him.

bends.ours: aliases.js cites the Morning Star case; credit has no verified snip of On Sense and Reference.
bends.theirs: Only the Begriffsschrift passage is verified; the 1892 text is not on disk.
